subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy choice for adult attention difficulties when stimulant diversion is a live concern
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29 year old man referred with lifelong inattention, disorganisation and restlessness, with clear evidence of impairment from primary school onwards confirmed by school reports and by his mother.

He has used methamphetamine intermittently for three years, most recently four weeks ago, and drinks six standard drinks on two nights a week. He has no psychotic symptoms and no mood disorder. He lives in a shared house where another resident has previously taken his prescribed medication without asking. His blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg, pulse 78 beats per minute, and his electrocardiogram and physical examination are normal. He is engaged with a drug and alcohol service and wants treatment for his attention difficulties.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Restless but cooperative, normal speech, no psychotic features, no tremor, normal cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, urine drug screen negative today, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacological approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Sertraline titrated over several weeks, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not treat inattention or hyperactivity and he has no depressive or anxiety disorder to justify one. Prescribing it would treat a diagnosis he does not have. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

options.text: Atomoxetine titrated over several weeks, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: A non stimulant avoids both the misuse potential and the diversion risk created by his housing situation, and it has no street value while remaining effective for core symptoms. Australian guidance favours a non stimulant when substance use is recent or the storage environment is insecure. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

options.text: No pharmacotherapy until he has been abstinent for twelve months, with continued engagement in the service
options.rationale: Withholding treatment for a year worsens the impairment that drives much of the substance use, and treating attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is associated with reduced rather than increased substance use. Abstinence is not a prerequisite for non stimulant treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

options.text: Modafinil taken each morning, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Modafinil is not approved for this indication in Australia and the adult evidence is weak, so it is not a substitute for an agent with an established effect. Choosing it would leave his core symptoms inadequately treated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Immediate release dexamfetamine three times daily, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Short acting stimulants carry the highest misuse and diversion potential of the available options and would be the least suitable choice in a house where medication has already been taken. Multiple daily doses also worsen adherence. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults requires symptoms present before the age of twelve with impairment in more than one setting, and corroborating evidence such as school reports or an informant history is central because retrospective self report alone is unreliable. Coexisting substance use is common, and untreated symptoms are themselves a risk factor for it, so treatment is not withheld until abstinence is achieved. Stimulants remain first line for most adults and are more effective than non stimulants, but the choice shifts when misuse or diversion is a genuine concern: lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug requiring enzymatic conversion and has lower misuse potential than immediate release preparations, while atomoxetine and guanfacine have essentially none. Housing where medication cannot be secured is a practical reason to choose a non stimulant. Cardiovascular assessment with blood pressure, pulse and a personal and family cardiac history precedes any stimulant, and prescribing in Australia is subject to state based authority requirements.
key_points: Childhood onset with corroborating evidence is required for the diagnosis
Treatment is not withheld until substance use abstinence is achieved
Lisdexamfetamine has lower misuse potential than immediate release stimulants
Atomoxetine and guanfacine have no misuse or diversion potential
Assess cardiovascular history and blood pressure before any stimulant
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically where the medication will be stored and who else has access, because diversion in shared housing is far more common than personal misuse, and that single practical question changes the prescription more often than the substance use history itself does.

sources.label: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

subtopic_detail: Parenteral sedation choice when verbal and oral measures have already failed in the department
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 34 year old man brought in by ambulance after threatening staff at a bus station. He is pacing, shouting, striking the walls and cannot be engaged in conversation.

De escalation has been attempted for twenty minutes by two experienced nurses and he has refused oral olanzapine wafers. Security is present and physical restraint is in place. His pulse is 126 beats per minute and blood pressure 148/90 mmHg taken during a brief window of cooperation, and his temperature measured tympanically is 37.1 degrees Celsius. He is known to the service with schizophrenia and has not taken his depot for three months. A capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L, and no intravenous access has been achieved. There is no history of cardiac disease and no electrocardiogram is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 not obtainable, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, shouting, striking walls, not engageable, no obvious injury, pupils equal
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L, no intravenous access, no electrocardiogram available, no previous electrocardiogram on file

lead_in: What is the most appropriate parenteral sedation?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine with intramuscular lorazepam together, with continuous monitoring after the doses are given
options.rationale: Combining parenteral olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine is specifically cautioned against because of reports of cardiorespiratory depression and death. If both are used they must be separated in time. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol with promethazine together, with continuous monitoring after the doses are given
options.rationale: This combination is used in some settings but causes more dystonia and prolonged sedation than droperidol, and promethazine adds anticholinergic burden without improving speed of onset. It is not the Australian first choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold parenteral sedation until an electrocardiogram can be obtained, continuing physical restraint meanwhile
options.rationale: Prolonged physical restraint carries its own risks of rhabdomyolysis, positional asphyxia and staff and patient injury, and an electrocardiogram cannot be obtained in a struggling patient anyway. Sedation is what makes the assessment possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam as a single dose, with continuous monitoring and a repeat dose if needed after fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Midazolam works quickly but causes more respiratory depression and over sedation than droperidol, and it is a second line agent or an adjunct rather than the preferred single agent. Airway complications in a restrained patient are the main hazard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol as a single dose, with continuous monitoring and a repeat dose if needed after fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Droperidol given intramuscularly is the Australian first line for acute behavioural disturbance, achieving sedation faster and more reliably than benzodiazepine monotherapy with less respiratory depression. Large Australian emergency studies found no clinically significant arrhythmia at these doses, so the absence of an electrocardiogram does not preclude its use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed in a graded way, beginning with environmental measures and verbal de escalation, moving to offered oral medication, and using parenteral sedation only when those have failed and there is risk to the patient or others. Australian emergency practice favours intramuscular droperidol as the single most effective first line agent, supported by randomised work from Australian emergency departments showing faster and more reliable sedation than midazolam with fewer airway events. Concern about corrected QT prolongation led to restricted use for many years, but subsequent prospective Australian data found no clinically significant arrhythmia at the doses used for sedation, and routine electrocardiography is not required before giving it in an emergency. Whichever agent is used, monitoring afterwards is mandatory and includes level of consciousness, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure and temperature, with a search for medical causes of the disturbance including hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury, intoxication and withdrawal.
key_points: De escalation and offered oral medication precede parenteral sedation
Intramuscular droperidol is the Australian first line parenteral agent
Routine electrocardiography is not required before emergency sedation
Avoid giving parenteral olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine
Monitor consciousness, respiration, saturation and temperature afterwards
explanation.pearls: Check a capillary glucose in every acutely disturbed patient before attributing the presentation to their psychiatric diagnosis, because hypoglycaemia, hypoxia and head injury all present as agitation and are the medical causes most often missed when a person is known to the mental health service.

subtopic_detail: Weight gain and impaired glucose handling one year into second generation antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26 year old woman one year after her first episode of psychosis, treated with olanzapine 15 mg daily. She has had no psychotic symptoms for eight months and has returned to part time study.

Her weight has risen from 62 kg to 78 kg over the year, her waist circumference is 96 cm, and her fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L on two occasions with a glycated haemoglobin of 44 mmol/mol. Fasting triglycerides are 2.6 mmol/L and high density lipoprotein cholesterol is 0.9 mmol/L. Her blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and her prolactin is normal. She has engaged with a dietitian and an exercise programme for four months without weight loss, and she is clear that she does not want to risk another episode of psychosis.

data_table.Examination: Weight 78 kg, waist circumference 96 cm, body mass index 29 kg/m2, no acanthosis nigricans, euthymic with no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.5) on two occasions, glycated haemoglobin 44 mmol/mol, fasting triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L (greater than 1.2), prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue olanzapine and start a statin for the lipid abnormality, with review of glucose in six months
options.rationale: Treating one downstream abnormality while the cause continues leaves the weight gain and glucose intolerance unaddressed, and a woman of childbearing potential on a statin needs contraceptive counselling as well. Lipid treatment may still be needed later but is not the first step. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and intensify the dietitian and exercise programme with monthly weight review
options.rationale: Lifestyle intervention has already run for four months without effect, and it is substantially less effective while the drug driving the weight gain continues. Repeating a failed strategy allows the metabolic abnormalities to progress to diabetes. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Discuss switching to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic risk, with close monitoring for relapse during the change
options.rationale: She has impaired fasting glucose and dyslipidaemia attributable to the agent with the highest metabolic liability, and lifestyle measures have already had a fair trial. Switching to an agent such as aripiprazole improves the metabolic profile while maintaining antipsychotic cover if the change is made gradually. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Halve the olanzapine dose and continue at that level, with review of weight and glucose in three months
options.rationale: Weight gain from this agent is only weakly dose related, so halving the dose gives little metabolic benefit while meaningfully raising the relapse risk in the first two years after a first episode. It combines the disadvantages of both options. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic entirely given eight months of remission, with monthly review for early relapse symptoms
options.rationale: Relapse rates after stopping treatment within two years of a first episode approach 80 percent, and each relapse is associated with poorer functional recovery. The metabolic problem is a reason to change the drug, not to stop treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: People with schizophrenia die fifteen to twenty years earlier than the general population, and most of that gap is cardiovascular rather than from suicide, so metabolic monitoring is a core part of psychiatric care rather than an afterthought. Second generation antipsychotics differ markedly in metabolic liability: clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest risk, quetiapine and risperidone are intermediate, and aripiprazole, lurasidone and ziprasidone are lowest. Australian guidance is to measure weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, at six and twelve weeks, and then at least annually. When abnormalities appear, the options are lifestyle intervention, switching to a lower risk agent, or adding metformin, which has reasonable evidence for attenuating antipsychotic associated weight gain. Switching must be done gradually with cross tapering and close relapse monitoring, and metformin is a reasonable alternative when the current agent is the only one that has controlled the illness, as is often the case with clozapine.
key_points: Cardiovascular disease, not suicide, drives most of the mortality gap
Clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest metabolic risk
Monitor weight, waist, blood pressure, glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks, then annually
Options are lifestyle change, switching agent, or adding metformin
Stopping antipsychotic treatment within two years of a first episode risks relapse in most patients
explanation.pearls: Add metformin rather than switching when the current agent is clozapine or is the only drug that has ever controlled the illness, starting at 500 mg daily and titrating, since it produces a modest but real reduction in weight and improves insulin sensitivity without risking the relapse that a cross taper can precipitate.

sources.label: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Broad ventricular complexes after a large ingestion of an older antidepressant
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 41 year old woman brought in ninety minutes after taking an estimated forty amitriptyline tablets with alcohol, found by her partner with an empty bottle.

She is drowsy but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12, her pupils are dilated, her skin is dry and flushed and her bladder is palpable. Her pulse is 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 132 milliseconds and a prominent R wave in lead aVR. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.31 and bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, her potassium is 3.6 mmol/L and her capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, palpable bladder, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram showing QRS 132 milliseconds with a prominent R wave in aVR, venous pH 7.31, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L, paracetamol level not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral activated charcoal given via nasogastric tube, repeated hourly while her conscious state is monitored
options.rationale: Charcoal is considered within an hour or two of a large ingestion but requires a protected airway in a drowsy patient, and it does not treat the cardiotoxicity already present. Decontamination never takes precedence over reversing the conduction abnormality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil given as a slow bolus, repeated until her conscious state and respiratory pattern improve
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which she has not taken, and it lowers the seizure threshold in mixed overdose, which is dangerous when the ingested drug is already proconvulsant. It has no role here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine given as a slow bolus, repeated to reverse the anticholinergic features she is showing
options.rationale: Physostigmine can precipitate asystole and seizures in tricyclic poisoning specifically, and it does nothing for the sodium channel blockade that is the lethal mechanism. The anticholinergic signs are a marker of the ingestion rather than the target of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone given as a loading infusion, repeated if the broad complexes persist on the monitor
options.rationale: Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics and amiodarone all block sodium channels themselves and worsen the toxicity that is causing the broad complexes. They are contraindicated in this poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate given as a bolus, repeated until the QRS narrows and the blood pressure improves
options.rationale: A QRS above 100 milliseconds indicates sodium channel blockade and predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmia, and hypertonic bicarbonate reverses it through both the sodium load and alkalinisation. It is given on the electrocardiographic finding rather than waiting for an arrhythmia to appear. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning remains one of the most lethal common overdoses because these drugs block fast sodium channels in the myocardium, in addition to their anticholinergic, antihistaminergic and alpha blocking effects. The electrocardiogram is both the diagnostic and the prognostic tool: a QRS duration above 100 milliseconds predicts seizures, above 160 milliseconds predicts ventricular arrhythmia, and a terminal R wave in lead aVR above 3 mm reflects the same conduction delay. Treatment is hypertonic sodium bicarbonate given in boluses titrated to narrowing of the QRS and to an arterial pH of about 7.50 to 7.55, supplemented by hyperventilation if the patient is intubated. Seizures are treated with benzodiazepines, hypotension with fluid and then noradrenaline, and antiarrhythmics that block sodium channels are contraindicated. Lipid emulsion and extracorporeal support are salvage options in refractory cardiac arrest.
key_points: QRS above 100 milliseconds indicates sodium channel blockade
Give hypertonic bicarbonate titrated to QRS narrowing, not to an arrhythmia
A terminal R wave in lead aVR is the same sign in another form
Amiodarone and class Ia and Ic agents are contraindicated
Use benzodiazepines for seizures and noradrenaline for refractory hypotension
explanation.pearls: Repeat the electrocardiogram every fifteen to thirty minutes during the first hours rather than relying on the presenting trace, because absorption continues and anticholinergic effects slow gastric emptying, so a patient who arrives with a normal QRS can deteriorate abruptly several hours after ingestion.

subtopic_detail: Lower limb clonus and agitation days after a second serotonergic agent is added for pain
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to review a 52 year old man on the surgical ward two days after a new analgesic was added following a laparotomy. He takes sertraline 150 mg daily for depression and was started on tramadol for post operative pain.

Over twelve hours he has become agitated and sweaty with diarrhoea. His pulse is 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 152/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air and temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. There is spontaneous clonus at both ankles, hyperreflexia more marked in the legs than the arms, and intermittent ocular clonus, with normal tone in the upper limbs. His creatine kinase is 640 units/L, white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L, and his wound is clean. He has never taken an antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 152/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Spontaneous ankle clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia greater in the legs than the arms, ocular clonus, normal upper limb tone, dilated pupils, wound clean
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 640 units/L (30-200), white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), blood cultures taken and pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the tramadol only, continue the sertraline, and give an antipyretic with observation over the next twelve hours
options.rationale: Stopping the precipitant is correct but leaving the other serotonergic drug in place may not resolve the toxicity, and antipyretics do not work because the hyperthermia comes from muscle activity rather than a raised hypothalamic set point. Twelve hours of observation risks progression to rigidity and rhabdomyolysis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Cease the tramadol and sertraline, give bromocriptine for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and cool actively
options.rationale: That syndrome develops over days rather than hours, produces lead pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, and requires exposure to a dopamine antagonist which he has never had. Bromocriptine is the wrong mechanism for this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Cease the tramadol and sertraline, give benzodiazepines and cooling, and add cyproheptadine if features persist
options.rationale: Lower limb predominant hyperreflexia with spontaneous and ocular clonus developing over hours after a second serotonergic drug is serotonin toxicity, and removal of both agents with benzodiazepine sedation is the treatment. Cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist reserved for moderate cases that do not settle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Continue the current medications, give intravenous antibiotics for sepsis, and repeat the septic screen in the morning
options.rationale: Sepsis does not cause clonus, ocular clonus or a lower limb reflex gradient, and his wound is clean with a barely raised white cell count. Cultures are reasonable but continuing both serotonergic drugs allows the toxicity to progress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Cease the tramadol and sertraline, give benzodiazepines and cooling, and add dantrolene if features persist
options.rationale: Dantrolene treats the sustained muscle contraction of malignant hyperthermia and is used in severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome, neither of which produces clonus or hyperreflexia. It does not address serotonin receptor overstimulation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a predictable consequence of excessive serotonergic activity rather than an idiosyncratic reaction, and it arises most often when two agents acting by different mechanisms are combined. Tramadol is a frequent Australian culprit because it is a serotonin reuptake inhibitor as well as an opioid and is commonly added to the medication of a patient already taking an antidepressant. The Hunter criteria formalise the diagnosis: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, spontaneous clonus alone is sufficient, as is inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia, or hyperthermia with hypertonia. Onset is within hours, and the lower limbs are affected more than the upper limbs. This gradient and the presence of clonus distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which follows dopamine antagonist exposure, develops over days, and produces generalised lead pipe rigidity with depressed reflexes. Treatment is withdrawal of the serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines, active cooling and supportive care, with cyproheptadine for moderate cases and paralysis with intubation for severe hyperthermia.
key_points: Clonus and hyperreflexia greater in the legs than the arms is the signature
Onset is within hours of adding or increasing a serotonergic agent
Tramadol is a common precipitant because it inhibits serotonin reuptake
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome gives rigidity with hyporeflexia over days
Treat with withdrawal, benzodiazepines and cooling; cyproheptadine if persistent
explanation.pearls: A temperature above 41 degrees Celsius in serotonin toxicity is an indication for immediate paralysis, intubation and active cooling rather than further pharmacological treatment, because the heat is generated by muscular hyperactivity and rhabdomyolysis with disseminated intravascular coagulation follows quickly once that threshold is crossed.
